aesthetic-hypertrophy.name: Aesthetic Engine: 5-Day Hypertrophy
aesthetic-hypertrophy.description: For experienced lifters who enjoy five gym days. Balanced upper/lower muscle building with extra shoulder work. Full gym; roughly 55–75 minutes per session.
guidelines: Train five days a week and keep two days free for recovery, ideally one between the second and third sessions. Add time between sessions if recovery suffers.
The listed sets are working sets. Warm up first, then use progressively heavier practice sets before your first heavy lifts.
Finish most sets with about 2 good repetitions left. Keep the same controlled range of motion; failure is not required.

When every set reaches the top of its rep range with clean form in two sessions, try the smallest available weight increase while aiming to keep the same reps. If reps or form suffer, use a smaller increase or repeat the previous load. Otherwise keep the weight and build reps.
Keep the plan for 6–8 weeks before judging progress. If fatigue accumulates or performance drops across several sessions, use fewer sets and lighter loads for a week. Do not train through pain.

guidelines: Train four days a week, ideally with a rest day between the second and third sessions. Rest 3 minutes on the main lifts, longer if needed; keep heavy sets controlled, never grinding to failure.

classic-ppl.name: Pure PPL: 6-Day Hypertrophy
classic-ppl.description: For experienced lifters who can consistently recover from six gym days. Two push, pull and leg sessions with distinct emphases. Full gym; about 45–65 minutes.
guidelines: Take one rest day each week. Choose the 4-day Upper/Lower plan if six days is hard to sustain. Pull days use supported rows, leaving heavy hip hinges to leg days.
On the assisted pull-up machine, log the counterweight; needing less assistance is progress. If bar dips bother your shoulders, shorten the range or edit the exercise to Assisted Dip Machine.

full-body-classic.description: A manageable starting point for beginners and returning lifters. Repeat key movement patterns instead of learning a new routine every day. Gym with dumbbells, bench, leg press and cables; about 40–55 minutes.
guidelines: Use non-consecutive days. For the first two weeks, leave 3–4 good repetitions in reserve and prioritize learning the setup over adding weight. Ask for help with unfamiliar equipment.
If you cannot do 5 push-ups yet, place your hands on a bench or edit Full Body C to Incline Push-up.

home-forge-dumbbells.name: Home Forge: 4-Day Dumbbells
home-forge-dumbbells.description: Upper/lower training with adjustable dumbbells and an adjustable bench; no cables, barbell or pull-up station. For lifters comfortable with the basics. About 40–60 minutes.
guidelines: Train four days a week, ideally with a rest day between the second and third sessions. Use a stable low platform for the front-foot-elevated split squat. If your dumbbells become too light, use the top of the rep range with controlled form; do not invent extra weight in the log.
Do single-leg calf raises on a step; once bodyweight is easy, hold a dumbbell on the working side and log it as added weight.

athletic-performance.name: Athletic Engine: 3-Day Strength & Power
athletic-performance.description: General strength and low-rep power practice for experienced lifters, not a sport-specific conditioning plan. Full gym with trap bar, kettlebell and low platform; about 50–65 minutes.
guidelines: Train on non-consecutive days and account for your sport sessions. Learn swings and push presses before using this plan. Use light-to-moderate loads on these two lifts and stop the set as soon as speed or technique drops, even before the target reps.
Do not apply automatic rep-range progression to swings or push presses: add load only while every repetition stays fast and controlled. This plan does not replace aerobic training or sport practice.

machine-foundation.name: Machine Foundation: 3-Day Full Body
machine-foundation.description: For beginners, returning lifters or anyone who prefers machine setups to free weights. Three repeatable full-body sessions using selectorized/sled machines and cables. About 40–55 minutes; check that your gym has the listed machines.
guidelines: Use non-consecutive days. Set the seat, pads and range of motion before loading; record the same machine’s load each time, since stack numbers differ between machines. Leave 3–4 repetitions in reserve while learning.

bodyweight-base.name: Bodyweight Base: 3-Day No Equipment
bodyweight-base.description: Full-body training at home without gym equipment: floor space, a wall or counter, a stable chair and a stair step. For beginners and returning lifters. Three short sessions of roughly 30–40 minutes.
guidelines: Train three days a week with a rest day after each session. Before each session, check that the chair or sofa cannot slide and that the step is stable.
Without a bar or other equipment, back and biceps work is limited and there is no direct hamstring curl. When you can, add a securely installed pull-up bar and move to Bar & Floor.
Progress push-ups by lowering the hand support step by step until you reach the floor. If you cannot do 3 floor push-ups yet, edit Full Body B to use Incline Push-up until you can.
The listed sets are working sets. Warm up first with a few minutes of easy movement, then do an easier practice set of the first exercise.
Finish most sets with about 2 good repetitions left. Keep the same controlled range of motion; failure is not required.

Log bodyweight sets with 0 added weight; the app shows them as BW. When every set reaches the top of its rep range with clean form in two sessions, make the exercise harder instead of adding endless reps: slow the lowering, use the harder variation named in these notes, or add a loaded backpack and log its weight as added load.
Keep the plan for 6–8 weeks before judging progress. If fatigue accumulates or performance drops across several sessions, use fewer sets and easier variations for a week. Do not train through pain.

bar-floor-calisthenics.name: Bar & Floor: 4-Day Calisthenics
bar-floor-calisthenics.description: Upper/lower bodyweight training with a pull-up bar, floor space, a stable chair and a stair step. For people who can already do at least 3 strict pull-ups or chin-ups. Four sessions of roughly 40–50 minutes.
guidelines: Train four days a week, alternating upper and lower body, ideally with a rest day between the second and third sessions. Before every session, check the bar’s fixing and weight limit; mount and dismount with a controlled step.

Start when you can do at least 3 strict pull-ups or chin-ups; until then, use Bodyweight Base. Nordic curls need a secure ankle anchor and knee padding: lower only as far as you can control and catch yourself with your hands.

A doorway bar does not allow rows, so upper-back and rear-shoulder work is limited. Progress push-ups to decline push-ups; progress pull-ups with a slower lowering or a loaded backpack logged as added weight.

Keep the plan for 6–8 weeks before judging progress. If fatigue accumulates or performance drops across several sessions, use fewer sets and easier variations for a week. Do not train through pain.
